column1: # Swedish name and word pronunciations for the Alice and Björn voices.
# Columns: word<TAB>phonemes[<TAB>word-only]. Phonemes use the NST/Kokoro symbols of the voice
# pack lexicon, with the stress mark directly before the stressed vowel.
# First-pass drafts for frequent names and book titles that the neural
# fallback misreads, mostly in stress. Compound titles follow the lexicon:
# main stress on the first part, secondary stress on the second. Not yet reviewed by ear. The corpus build adds the
# genitive -s form unless word-only is set. Homographs need that flag when the
# extra -s spelling has another meaning, such as ko (cow) and Kos (a place).
# Corrections in the review tool take
# priority over word entries, but not over phrases (see the end of the file).
# Joses already ends in s; its possessive apostrophe does not make it Jose + s.
# Jordán has stress and a long a on its second syllable ("Betoning av bibliska
# namn", De apokryfiska böckerna 1921, p. 277). NST's name row jˈoːɖan is the
# modern given name, which sounds English.
# Betsaída: stress on the ai diphthong (same appendix, New Testament rule 1).
# The neural fallback reads ai as ä in these names. Final -ai and the dual
# -aim are a + i, as in Barsillai, Mahanaim, and NST's Efraim. Stress follows
# the appendix's Old Testament rules: first syllable in names of two or three
# Stress from "Betoning av bibliska namn" (De apokryfiska böckerna 1921,
# p. 277-278): its stressed examples, such as Abinádab, Rehábeam, Daríus,
# and Dekápolis, and its endings. Before -ael, -eel, -iel, -uel, -iab, -eam,
# and -oam the stress falls on the syllable before the ending (Mehújael,
# Gámliel). Before -pater, -pator, -patris, -polis, and -ius it falls on the
# syllable before the ending, and before -anus, -ene, -itis, -nika, -nice, and
# -nikus on the next-to-last syllable. These rows correct names that the
# neural fallback stresses elsewhere or shortens by a syllable.
# The appendix's general rules for corpus names without an NST entry. Old
# Testament: names of two or three syllables are stressed on the first
# syllable, unless they end in -a or the last vowel follows two or more
# consonants (then the next-to-last); longer names on the next-to-last.
# Apocrypha and New Testament: the next-to-last syllable before two or more
# consonants or a diphthong; names also in the Old Testament keep its stress.
# The neural fallback mostly stresses the last syllable (Abdon, Ebal), reads ae
# as ä (Baesa, Jaeser), or spells out short names (Us, Kus). Hebrew ae, ee and
# aa are two vowels, as in Jael and Jaasiel. The psalm titles' own accents
# (Gittít, Alamót) give their stress. Final -ai is a + i, as above.
# SO gives speˋtälsk and speˋtälska: stress on the second syllable. NST and the
# voice stress spe- like a compound, with a long e or, in spetälskan, a short ä.
# SAOL: the interjection välan is stressed on -an; the colloquial adverb on väl-.
# Every välan in this Bible is the interjection.
# SO: välsigna [-siŋ´na]. NST lacks these two forms, and the fallback reads väl- as "well".
# Vowel length: NST incorrectly gives these forms a long u.
# Homographs. The voice pack's lexicon keeps one pronunciation per spelling and
# often took a name's, an abbreviation's, or another word's, such as "Han" for
# "han" and the genitive of "ko" for "kors". Each entry is the NST alternative
# for the word's sense in this Bible, chosen from
# Further homographs, checked against every occurrence in the Swedish corpus.
# Words whose sense changes between verses. A row with a bracketed word is a
# phrase: the phonemes apply to that word wherever the whole phrase occurs, and
# the phrase outranks a per-word entry or review correction. The phrases cover
# every sv1917 occurrence of the less frequent sense, or of the sense the voice
# "hov": past tense of "häva", except a royal court.
# "förlåten": the voice says "forgiven"; these phrases are the temple veil.
# "bete": the voice says the noun (pasture); these phrases are the verb "bete sig".
# "dans" is a dance, except the tribe of Dan: "Dans stam", "Dans barn".
# "ana": the name Ana, except the verb "ana" (suspect).
# "förband": the verb "förbinda", except the noun (bandage) in Ezekiel 30:21.
# "väl": SO separates 1väl "well" [vä´l], with a long ä, from 2väl [väl´], with a
# short ä. 2väl is the modal "surely" or "I suppose", as in "Kan väl en blind leda
# en blind?" (Luke 6:39), and the concession "väl ..., men". It is the majority in
# this Bible, so it is the word's reading. These phrases mark the long "well".
# They come from a reading of all 645 occurrences; their neighbors have no corrections of their own.
